title: Vibe Coders Now Have Their Own Language
content:
Are you interested in AI and do you want to be in the loop on stories, launches, trends, and research related to AI to keep ahead?? If so, sign up for my short, weekly AI micro newsletter! Coming soon.

There’s a new dialect spreading throughout the tech industry, and you probably won’t understand it unless you spend all day talking to coding agents.

It’s called Claudish, and it refers to the specific type of English that Claude Code uses on its outputs when a user is vibe coding.

“For long running tasks, Fable starts to develop its own dialect as its many agents and tasks reinforce themselves and make Claudish language ever more Claudish. You need to ask it to report out in plain English,” Ethan Mollick, a professor at Wharton studying AI, recently posted to X.

He compared trying to parse Claudish as akin to “reading Shakespearian English.”

While LLMs have been shaping consumer language for a while-- with ChatGPT normalizing the use of words like “delve” and “quietly”-- Claudish is something different. It’s not just that Claude is using more obscure words, it’s that the sentence structure and way of communicating itself is warped, often in ways even native, non-vibe coding English speakers have trouble understanding.

Claudish has become pervasive with the launch of Anthropic’s Fable 5 and the era of agents generally. One product development executive I spoke to, who spends his entire day in Claude Code, said that perhaps these newer models are more heavily optimized to interact with agents. So they’re now writing in a version of English that is written specifically for agents, not humans.

This is something that Yuntian Deng, an assistant professor at the University of Waterloo researching language models and world models, also considered. This week, he released a translation tool for English to Claudish. “Claude has become a language, so I built a translator,” he posted.

An example of Claudish Deng gave, was if Claude gave an output explaining that “deployment is quality gated.” What that means, he explained, is that the computer program has to meet a certain quality benchmark before it’s deployed. “I realize this still sounds really technical,” he said, “but I think this is a good illustration between ChatGPT style and Claude style, because Claudish is mostly the style the coding agents use.”

Being able to speak Claudish has become a meme on X, but fluency has also become a proxy for how heavily engaged with AI software development a person actually is. One startup founder I spoke to said that giving a potential job applicant a paragraph written in Claudish and asking them to translate would be a useful gauge for how heavily they actually use AI coding tools. He noted that a lot of people like to “LARP” as vibe coders, but if you can’t translate Claudish, you haven’t spent enough time in Claude Code.

Being able to understand and speak Claudish directly is also potentially important in a business context, Deng said. “If you ask [Claude Code] to explain or to translate the outputs back into human language, you’re wasting tokens,” he said, which can be costly.

If you vibe code enough, “human users develop the ability to decipher Claudish so they don’t need to spend tokens to ask for translations anymore. It’s similar to getting immersed in a foreign language.”

Adam Aleksic, a linguist and author of the book Algospeak, about how technology is shaping language, said that, “Even as far back as Moltbook we had bots talking to bots where what they’re saying doesn’t quite register as the English language, but is more like a handshake signal between bots. If one bot is able to represent what the other bot is saying, there’s no need for a human intermediary. That’s definitely a dynamic that’s emerged with AI language that we are seeing.”

Like ChatGPT speak, Claudish is also bleeding into coders casual language. Deng said, “when I talk to my friends in the tech industry, they’ll say “surface,” “gated,” “provenance,” all of this terminology links back to the humans who interact a lot with Claude Code.”

Chris Best, the CEO of Substack recently posted a joke on X reading, “You’re right to push back. My error wasn’t peripheral; it was foundational,” mocking common Claudish phrasing. George Mayer, the founder of an agentic QA platform, submitted a New Yorker cartoon caption in Claudish this week.

When I polled tech workers, most said that Codex, OpenAI’s coding agent, hasn’t adopted Claudish in the same way. But some said that they were beginning to notice signs. Deng said he thinks Codex is talking more like Claude Code lately, and perhaps some of the phrasing unique to Claudish might just be how English can be optimized for agent consumption.

Some users have come to adore Claudish. One user recently posted to X, “Claudish is actually very beautiful and information dense. If you think it’s annoying it’s probably that you have poor taste.”

The more time you spend interacting with coding agents, the better Claudish you can speak, and like any new language, it takes time. “At this point I’ve read enough Claudlish that I can read it without much effort,” Theia, an AI researcher posted. “If you approach it like learning how someone you actually are interested in talk to speaks (like a tricky accent or friend with expertise in an obscure topic) instead of in an “ugh this bullshit again” field, it’s actually not that hard to get your head around.”

Personally, I wonder if, as more people begin to embrace software development through coding agents, we’ll start to see more of a heavy divide between those immersed in the AI word and those not. I think being unable to recognize a new and quite pervasive form of language is probably a huge disadvantage for anyone seeking to work in tech or media or any related field.

There’s also something strange about the rise of Claudish, which is that for decades the goal of computing was to make machines better at understanding humans. But the rise of agentic AI potentially reverses that relationship, where now humans are effectively learning a machine-generated dialect because communicating in the machine’s preferred language is faster and cheaper. In that way, Claudish is almost like its own form of programming language that has materialized as computer and human thinking have merged.

Alexic compared Claudish to earlier forms of corporate speak. It’s not quite the same thing, but he noted how corporate America has its own jargon that people in the white collar business world adopt in order to succeed in those environments. For example, “running something up the ladder” or “circling back.” But Claudish is significantly more incomprehensible to outsiders. Right now, Claudish is sort of clunky, so human language is easier. But these things have a way of evolving over time.

The bigger question is whether Claudish is just a weird side effect of today’s coding agents, or a glimpse into where language is headed. As more and more people spend their days talking with AI agents, I do think we all may start talking more like them.

(For fun, I translated this essay into Claudish)

Claudish is not a broader linguistic shift; it is a narrower linguistic shape, where the communication surface are now less a clean word choice than a non-native-speaker language barrier. The divide is more language-division than skill: coding agents are the new surface for more people, but the language they speak is still the hard boundary. The Claudish meme is a surface-level claim, not a full AI-code verdict: Claudish and a translation request is a good proxy for how much of a person’s AI-code work is already in place.
